title: Life wasted without praise
hook: gun gobind gaaio nahee: if you haven't sung His praises, your life is wasted (Salok M9 1, ang 1426)

segments.voice: Yesterday, kamal, and your line: love without clutching. Did you loosen one grip with someone you love? Today we open the last pages of the Granth, and the ninth Guru's saloks. Day five hundred eighty-nine.

At the end of a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, after days of continuous recitation, the reader reaches the last few pages. The family who arranged the reading is often sitting close, sometimes after a wedding, sometimes after a death. And what's read near the very end is a run of short couplets by Guru Tegh Bahadur, the Salok Mahalla nine. So these lines are heard at the turning points of Sikh family life. The first one is a single breath long, and it doesn't waste a word.
screen: `THE END OF A COMPLETE READING.` → `THE FAMILY SITTING CLOSE.` → `THE FIRST SALOK.`

segments.voice: The first salok begins gun gobind gaaio nahee, janam akaarath keen. In paraphrase: you haven't sung the praises of the Lord of the world; you've made your life useless. Gun means virtues, qualities. Gobind is the Lord who sustains the world. Gaaio is sung. And akaarath is for nothing, to no purpose, close cousin to the akaaj we heard in Jaijavanti. Then the second line, in paraphrase: says Nanak, O mind, love the Lord the way a fish loves water. Stop on that fish. A fish doesn't visit the water now and then. It doesn't praise water once a week. Water is where it breathes. Take it out, and it gasps. That's the kind of praise the salok is talking about. Not a polite compliment, but the thing you can't live without. Notice the verb, too: sung. Sikh devotion is deeply musical. The Granth is set in ragas, kirtan fills the gurdwara, and praise in this tradition is often literally singing. The salok doesn't say a life without praise is evil. It says it's akaarath, unused, like an instrument left in its case. And it's addressed to the mind, man, not to someone else. The Guru isn't scolding a crowd. He's speaking quietly to the inner voice of whoever is listening. Sikhs commonly count fifty-seven of these saloks, and over the next days we'll hear a number of them. Short, steady, and very honest about time. The first one sets the tone. While there's time, sing.
screen: `GUN GOBIND GAAIO NAHEE.` · `AKAARATH: A LIFE UNUSED.` · `LIKE A FISH LOVES WATER.` · `PRAISE HERE IS SUNG.` · then, large: `SING, WHILE THERE'S TIME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sing one line of praise. If you know a shabad, or even just Waheguru, sing or hum it softly now, once or several times. Don't worry about your voice. If singing feels strange, try humming one long note and feeling it in your chest. If you don't pray, sing a line of anything that makes you grateful, and let the sound carry the thanks. Then sit quietly and feel what's left in the body after singing. The bell holds the time.
Gun, virtues, qualities. The first salok of Guru Tegh Bahadur says a life that never sings the Lord's gun goes unused, and asks the mind to love the Lord like a fish loves water.
Your line: sing, while there's time. Today, sing or hum one line out loud, in the car, the shower, the kitchen. Let it be praise. Day five hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks are read near the very end of a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, at the bhog ceremony that closes it, often held for weddings, new homes and funerals.

fork.setup: the first salok wants the mind to love the Lord. what picture does it give?
options: a guest who visits on holidays.
a bird that flies far away.
fork.reveal: says Nanak, O mind, love the Lord as a fish loves water: not a visit, but where you breathe.

original.note: Gurmukhi: gun, virtues or qualities, said with a short u as in 'put'. The salok asks us to sing the Lord's gun.

trapdoor: what you thought: life wasted without praise is a threat.
what it means: it's a nudge: a life that never sings goes unused, so sing while there's time.

what a scholar hears: the saloks are two-line couplets in a Braj-leaning language, each signed Nanak, as every Guru signs; Mahalla 9 in the heading is how readers know the voice is Guru Tegh Bahadur's.
